How this collection was made

All 19 PDF pages were inspected. 54 question or subquestion entries from seven Quantum Chemistry papers match the uploaded syllabus. Questions are grouped by unit, retaining their original paper, number and marks. Repeated questions stay as separate entries.

The readable question text is transcribed; “Original printed question” opens the source paper excerpt, including its supplied equations. Typographical errors and missing assumptions are flagged outside the model answer. These are worked model solutions, not an official answer key.

Origin of the Quantum Theory of Matter

Syllabus: Franck–Hertz experiment; photoelectric effect; Compton effect; black body radiation; Planck’s law; Wien’s law; Bohr’s theory; atomic spectra.

10 matching entries

Test I · September 2023 · Q1(i)
PDF page 1 · 1 mark · Unit 1
Question

In the atomic spectrum of hydrogen, the Balmer series occurs in the visible and near UV regions.

Original printed question · PDF page 1

Ans. 1(i)

True. Balmer lines arise from transitions n≥3→2. The low-n lines are visible; the series converges at about 364.6 nm, in the near ultraviolet.

1/λ=RH(1/2²−1/n²).
Test I · September 2023 · Q1(ii)
PDF page 1 · 1 mark · Unit 1
Question

A blackbody is one which absorbs all the frequencies but emits none.

Original printed question · PDF page 1

Ans. 1(ii)

False. A black body absorbs all incident radiation, but at any nonzero temperature it also emits radiation. It is an ideal absorber and emitter. Its equilibrium spectrum depends only on temperature.

Test I · September 2023 · Q1(iii)
PDF page 1 · 1 mark · Unit 1
Question

The Wein’s displacement law is independent of temperature.

Original printed question · PDF page 1

Ans. 1(iii)

False. Wien’s displacement law explicitly relates the wavelength of maximum spectral intensity to absolute temperature:

λmaxT = b = 2.898 × 10−3 m K.

Thus λmax decreases as T increases; the law is not independent of temperature.

Test I · September 2023 · Q1(iv)
PDF page 1 · 1 mark · Unit 1
Question

The radius of the first Bohr orbit is 0.5529 Å.

Original printed question · PDF page 1

Ans. 1(iv)

False. The radius of the first Bohr orbit of hydrogen is

a₀ = 4πε₀ℏ²/(mₑe²) = 0.529 Å (approximately),

rather than the printed 0.5529 Å.

Mid Term · October 2023 · Q1(i)
PDF page 2 · 1 mark · Unit 1
Question

At the stopping potential, the initial K.E. of the electrons is equal to the P.E.

Original printed question · PDF page 2

Ans. 1(i)

True for the most energetic photoelectrons. The retarding electric field removes their maximum initial kinetic energy. At stopping potential Vₛ,

Kmax=eVₛ=hν−Φ.

Electrons with smaller kinetic energy are stopped before this potential is reached.

Mid Term · October 2023 · Q1(ii)
PDF page 2 · 1 mark · Unit 1
Question

A blackbody is one which absorbs all the frequencies but emits none.

Original printed question · PDF page 2

Ans. 1(ii)

False. A black body absorbs all incident radiation, but at any nonzero temperature it also emits radiation. It is an ideal absorber and emitter. Its equilibrium spectrum depends only on temperature.

Mid Term · October 2023 · Q1(iii)
PDF page 2 · 1 mark · Unit 1
Question

The phenomenon of ultraviolet catastrophe is associated with blackbody radiation.

Original printed question · PDF page 2

Ans. 1(iii)

True. The classical Rayleigh–Jeans law predicts uν=8πν²kBT/c³. It diverges as frequency increases, yielding infinite integrated energy. This contradiction is the ultraviolet catastrophe. Planck’s quantized-energy law removes it.

Mid Term · October 2023 · Q1(iv)
PDF page 2 · 1 mark · Unit 1
Question

The threshold frequency is related to the work function by the eqn. hν₀ = Φ.

Original printed question · PDF page 2

Ans. 1(iv)

True. At threshold, the emitted electron has zero maximum kinetic energy. Einstein’s equation hν=Φ+Kmax therefore reduces to

Φ=hν₀.

Operators and Wave Functions in Quantum Mechanics

Syllabus: Operator principles; Hamiltonian and Hermitian operators; postulates; Schrödinger equation; free particle; particle in a box (one and three dimensions).

20 matching entries

Test I · September 2023 · Q1(v)
PDF page 1 · 1 mark · Unit 3
Question

ψ = sin x is an acceptable wave function. However, it is not normalized.

Original printed question · PDF page 1
The paper gives no domain or boundary conditions. The expected finite-domain interpretation and the whole-line limitation are both stated.

Ans. 1(v)

True for the intended finite-domain example. On 0≤x≤π, sin x is finite, continuous, single-valued and satisfies zero endpoint values. Its norm is ∫₀πsin²x dx = π/2, not 1.

ψnormalized(x) = √(2/π) sin x, 0≤x≤π.

On the whole real line, sin x is not square-integrable and is not a normalizable bound-state wave function.

Test I · September 2023 · Q1(vii)
PDF page 1 · 1 mark · Unit 3
Question

The square root (√) is not a linear operator but it is a Hermitian operator.

Original printed question · PDF page 1
This refers to taking the pointwise square root of a function. A spectral square root of a positive self-adjoint linear operator is a different construction.

Ans. 1(vii)

False. The pointwise operation T[f]=√f is nonlinear: generally √(f+g)≠√f+√g. A Hermitian observable is a linear operator with Â†=Â, so this nonlinear pointwise operation is not a Hermitian quantum-mechanical operator.

Test I · September 2023 · Q2
PDF page 1 · 2 marks · Unit 3
Question

Write the expression for the following operator: (d/dx x + x)².

Original printed question · PDF page 1
Operator order matters: D acts on everything to its right. If the first term were instead intended as XD, the answer would differ; the solution retains the order shown in the scan.

Ans. 2

Let D=d/dx and X denote multiplication by x. Read the printed product as (DX+X)². Since DX=XD+1, set B=XD+X+1. Acting on a test function f,

Bf=xf′+(x+1)f.
B²f = x d[xf′+(x+1)f]/dx +(x+1)[xf′+(x+1)f]
=x²f″+(2x²+3x)f′+(x²+3x+1)f.

(DX+X)²=x²D²+(2x²+3x)D+(x²+3x+1).

Test I · September 2023 · Q3
PDF page 1 · 5 marks · Unit 3
Question

Find out the average value of position of a particle in a one dimensional box of length ‘a’. (Hint: ψ = √(2/a) sin(nπx/a).)

Original printed question · PDF page 1

Ans. 3

The normalized eigenfunction for a box extending from x=0 to x=a is ψₙ(x)=√(2/a) sin(nπx/a). The expectation of position is

⟨x⟩ = ∫₀a ψₙ*(x) x ψₙ(x) dx = (2/a)∫₀ax sin²(nπx/a) dx.

Using sin²θ=(1−cos2θ)/2,

⟨x⟩ = (1/a)∫₀ax dx − (1/a)∫₀ax cos(2nπx/a) dx.

Let k=2nπ/a. The second integral equals [x sin(kx)/k + cos(kx)/k²]₀a=0 because sin(2nπ)=0 and cos(2nπ)=cos0=1.

⟨x⟩ = (1/a)[x²/2]₀a = a/2.

⟨x⟩=a/2 for every stationary box state. The average position lies at the centre.

Test I · September 2023 · Q5
PDF page 1 · 4 marks · Unit 3
Question

What do you mean by a Hermitian Operator? Prove that the eigenvalues of a Hermitian Operator are real.

Original printed question · PDF page 1

Ans. 5

An operator Â is Hermitian if its adjoint equals itself on its specified domain. Equivalently, for admissible functions φ and ψ,

∫φ*(Âψ)dτ = ∫(Âφ)*ψ dτ, or Â†=Â.

Let Âψ=aψ with ψ≠0. Then ⟨ψ|Âψ⟩=a⟨ψ|ψ⟩. Hermiticity also gives ⟨ψ|Âψ⟩=⟨Âψ|ψ⟩=a*⟨ψ|ψ⟩.

(a−a*)⟨ψ|ψ⟩=0.

Since the norm of a nonzero eigenfunction is positive, a=a*.

Every eigenvalue of a Hermitian operator is real. ∎

Test I · September 2023 · Q6
PDF page 1 · 2 marks · Unit 3
Question

Consider two wave functions Ψ₁ and Ψ₂, and write mathematical expressions to indicate the following: (i) Normalization Condition (ii) Orthogonality Condition.

Original printed question · PDF page 1

Ans. 6

(i) Normalization: each individual wave function has total probability one:

∫|Ψ₁|²dτ=1, ∫|Ψ₂|²dτ=1.

(ii) Orthogonality: their overlap vanishes:

∫Ψ₁*Ψ₂dτ=0.

Together, for an orthonormal set, ∫Ψᵢ*Ψⱼdτ=δᵢⱼ. The integration is over the entire allowed configuration space.

Mid Term · October 2023 · Q1(vii)
PDF page 2 · 1 mark · Unit 3
Question

The eigenfunctions of a Hermitian operator corresponding to different eigenvalues are orthonormal.

Original printed question · PDF page 2

Ans. 1(vii)

True with the usual normalized-eigenfunction convention. Eigenfunctions of a Hermitian operator belonging to distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal. They may each be normalized to unit norm, yielding an orthonormal set.

a≠b ⇒ ⟨ψa|ψb⟩=0; ⟨ψa|ψa⟩=1 after normalization.

Orthogonality is automatic; unit normalization is a separate choice. Without that convention, “orthonormal” is stronger than what the theorem alone guarantees.

Mid Term · October 2023 · Q1(viii)
PDF page 2 · 1 mark · Unit 3
Question

A particle in a 3D box with quantum numbers 1, 1 and 2 is triply degenerate.

Original printed question · PDF page 2
Equal box lengths are needed for this degeneracy; they are implicit in the expected answer.

Ans. 1(viii)

True for a cubical box. E=(h²/8ma²)(nₓ²+nᵧ²+n𝓏²). The permutations (1,1,2), (1,2,1) and (2,1,1) give the same sum 6 and three distinct states. Hence degeneracy=3. A general rectangular box need not have these equal energies.

Mid Term · October 2023 · Q1(x)
PDF page 2 · 1 mark · Unit 3
Question

The lowest energy of a particle moving in a one dimensional box of length ‘a’ is given by h²/8ma².

Original printed question · PDF page 2

Ans. 1(x)

True. For an infinite box of length a, Eₙ=n²h²/(8ma²), n=1,2,… . Thus the ground state n=1 has E₁=h²/(8ma²), rather than zero.

Mid Term · Autumn 2024 · Q4(b)
PDF page 3 · 3 marks · Unit 3
Question

Determine A so that the function is normalized. [ψ = Ax exp(−x²/2).]

Original printed question · PDF page 3

Ans. 4(b)

Impose normalization over the real line:

1 = ∫−∞∞|ψ|²dx = |A|²∫−∞∞x²e−x²dx.

Differentiate the Gaussian integral ∫e−αx²dx=√(π/α) with respect to α. At α=1 this gives ∫x²e−x²dx=√π/2.

|A|²(√π/2)=1 ⇒ |A|²=2/√π.

Taking A real and positive, A=√2/π1/4. An arbitrary overall phase gives the same physical state.

Mid Term · Autumn 2024 · Q7(i)
PDF page 3 · 3 marks · Unit 3
Question

Check whether the following operators commute or not: [x, d/dx].

Original printed question · PDF page 3

Ans. 7(i)

Let X denote multiplication by x and D=d/dx. Apply the commutator to an arbitrary differentiable function f:

[X,D]f = x f′ − d(xf)/dx = xf′−f−xf′=−f.

[X,D]=−1 (the negative identity operator). The operators do not commute.

Mid Term · Autumn 2024 · Q7(ii)
PDF page 3 · 3 marks · Unit 3
Question

Check whether the following operators commute or not: [d/dx, d²/dx²].

Original printed question · PDF page 3

Ans. 7(ii)

For a function with at least three derivatives,

[D,D²]f = D(D²f)−D²(Df)=f‴−f‴=0.

[d/dx,d²/dx²]=0; the operators commute on their common domain.

Mid Term · September 2022 · Q2
PDF page 6 · 1 mark · Unit 3
Question

The lowest energy of a particle moving in a one dimensional box of length ‘a’ is given by (i) 3h²/8ma² (ii) 2h²/8ma² (iii) h²/8ma² (iv) h²/6ma².

Original printed question · PDF page 6

Ans. 2

Correct option: (iii). The allowed energies are Eₙ=n²h²/(8ma²). The smallest allowed n is 1, so E₁=h²/(8ma²).

Mid Term · September 2022 · Q3
PDF page 6 · 1 mark · Unit 3
Question

The lowest energy of a particle moving in a cubical box of length ‘a’ is given by (i) 6h²/8ma² (ii) 9h²/8ma² (iii) h²/8ma² (iv) 3h²/8ma².

Original printed question · PDF page 6

Ans. 3

Correct option: (iv). In a cubic infinite box, E=(h²/8ma²)(nₓ²+nᵧ²+n𝓏²). Each quantum number is at least 1, so the ground state (1,1,1) has

E111=3h²/(8ma²).
Mid Term · September 2022 · Q4
PDF page 6 · 1 mark · Unit 3
Question

The energy state of particle moving in a three dimensional box of length ‘a’ having the quantum numbers 2, 2 and 1 is (i) doubly degenerate (ii) non degenerate (iii) triply degenerate (iv) none.

Original printed question · PDF page 6
The degeneracy assumes equal side lengths.

Ans. 4

Correct option: (iii), for a cube. The states (2,2,1), (2,1,2) and (1,2,2) all have nₓ²+nᵧ²+n𝓏²=9, and no other positive-integer triples give that sum. Thus the degeneracy is 3.

Mid Term · September 2022 · Q5
PDF page 6 · 1 mark · Unit 3
Question

State which of the following functions are acceptable as wave functions: (i) ψ=x (ii) ψ=sin x (iii) ψ=eˣ (iv) ψ=x².

Original printed question · PDF page 6
The original question does not specify a domain or boundary conditions. Do not equate “finite somewhere” with an acceptable physical wave function.

Ans. 5

Expected option: (ii), ψ=sin x, under the finite-box interpretation. On 0≤x≤π it is finite, continuous, square-integrable and vanishes at both boundaries. After multiplying by √(2/π), it is normalized.

On that same box, x, eˣ and x² fail the required zero endpoint conditions. On the whole real line none of the four is square-integrable; therefore no unique domain-independent answer exists.

Mid Term · September 2022 · Q10
PDF page 6 · 1 mark · Unit 3
Question

The Hamiltonian operator describes the total energy of a system.

Original printed question · PDF page 6

Ans. 10

True. The Hamiltonian represents total energy. For a single nonrelativistic particle, Ĥ=−(ℏ²/2m)∇²+V=T̂+V̂. A stationary eigenstate satisfies Ĥψ=Eψ.

4

Wave Mechanics of Simple Systems

Syllabus: One-dimensional harmonic oscillator; rigid rotator; hydrogen atom; angular momentum.

24 matching entries

Test I · September 2023 · Q1(vi)
PDF page 1 · 1 mark · Unit 4
Question

The square of the angular momentum operators always commute with its components.

Original printed question · PDF page 1

Ans. 1(vi)

True. Define L²=Lₓ²+Lᵧ²+L𝓏². Using [Lᵢ,Lⱼ]=iℏεᵢⱼₖLₖ,

[L²,Lₓ] = [Lᵧ²,Lₓ]+[L𝓏²,Lₓ] = −iℏ(LᵧL𝓏+L𝓏Lᵧ)+iℏ(L𝓏Lᵧ+LᵧL𝓏)=0.

Cyclic interchange gives [L²,Lᵧ]=[L²,L𝓏]=0. Hence the square commutes with every component.

Test I · September 2023 · Q4
PDF page 1 · 5 marks · Unit 4
Question

A certain system is described by the Hamiltonian operator H = −d²/dx² + x². Show that ψ = Ax exp(−x²/2) is eigenfunction of H; determine the eigenvalue.

Original printed question · PDF page 1

Ans. 4

Given Ĥ=−d²/dx²+x² and ψ=Axe−x²/2, differentiate:

ψ′=A(1−x²)e−x²/2,
ψ″=A(x³−3x)e−x²/2.
Ĥψ = −A(x³−3x)e−x²/2 + Ax³e−x²/2 = 3Axe−x²/2 = 3ψ.

ψ is an eigenfunction of Ĥ with eigenvalue 3 (in the dimensionless units of the stated operator).

Mid Term · October 2023 · Q1(ix)
PDF page 2 · 1 mark · Unit 4
Question

The simple harmonic oscillator was used as a model to explain rotation and vibration of molecules.

Original printed question · PDF page 2

Ans. 1(ix)

False. The harmonic oscillator models molecular vibration near equilibrium. Molecular rotation is modeled by the rigid rotator. The statement incorrectly attributes both motions to the oscillator.

Mid Term · October 2023 · Q2
PDF page 2 · 3 marks · Unit 4
Question

The l = 0 to l = 1 transition for CO (¹²C¹⁶O) occurs at 1.153×10⁵ MHz. Calculate the bond length in CO.

Original printed question · PDF page 2

Ans. 2

For a rigid diatomic rotator, El=ℏ²l(l+1)/(2I), with I=μr². The l=0→1 transition has ΔE=ℏ²/I=hν.

I = h/(4π²ν), r = √[h/(4π²μν)].

For ¹²C¹⁶O, μ=(12×16)/(12+16) u=(48/7)u=1.13866×10−26 kg. The given frequency is 1.153×10⁵ MHz=1.153×10¹¹ Hz.

I=6.62607×10−34/[4π²(1.153×10¹¹)]
=1.45568×10−46 kg m².
r = √[(1.45568×10−46)/(1.13866×10−26)]
=1.13067×10−10 m.

CO bond length ≈1.13 Å (using isotope masses approximated by their mass numbers).

Mid Term · October 2023 · Q3(a)
PDF page 2 · 5 marks · Unit 4
Question

Prove the following: The square of the angular momentum and its x-component can be specified simultaneously.

Original printed question · PDF page 2

Ans. 3(a)

The fundamental relations are [Lₓ,Lᵧ]=iℏL𝓏, [Lᵧ,L𝓏]=iℏLₓ and [L𝓏,Lₓ]=iℏLᵧ. Apply [A²,B]=A[A,B]+[A,B]A:

[L²,Lₓ]=−iℏ(LᵧL𝓏+L𝓏Lᵧ)+iℏ(L𝓏Lᵧ+LᵧL𝓏)=0.

Thus L² and Lₓ commute and possess a common eigenbasis. A simultaneous eigenfunction obeys L²ψ=l(l+1)ℏ²ψ and Lₓψ=mₓℏψ.

The square of angular momentum and its x-component can be specified simultaneously. ∎

Mid Term · October 2023 · Q3(b)
PDF page 2 · 5 marks · Unit 4
Question

Prove the following: The step-up operator do not commute with the z-component of angular momentum operator.

Original printed question · PDF page 2

Ans. 3(b)

Define the step-up operator L₊=Lₓ+iLᵧ. Then

[L𝓏,L₊]=[L𝓏,Lₓ]+i[L𝓏,Lᵧ]
=iℏLᵧ+i(−iℏLₓ)=ℏ(Lₓ+iLᵧ)=ℏL₊.
[L₊,L𝓏]=−ℏL₊≠0.

Accordingly, L₊ changes the magnetic quantum number: L₊|l,m⟩=ℏ√[l(l+1)−m(m+1)]|l,m+1⟩.

L₊ and L𝓏 do not commute. ∎

Mid Term · October 2023 · Q4
PDF page 2 · 2 marks · Unit 4
Question

Write down the expression for the Hamiltonian of a one dimensional Harmonic Oscillator.

Original printed question · PDF page 2

Ans. 4

For a particle of mass m with displacement x from equilibrium, the restoring potential is V(x)=½kx²=½mω²x², where ω=√(k/m). The Hamiltonian is kinetic plus potential energy:

Ĥ = −(ℏ²/2m) d²/dx² + ½mω²x².

The allowed energies are Ev=(v+½)ℏω, v=0,1,2,… .

Mid Term · October 2023 · Q5
PDF page 2 · 15 marks · Unit 4
Question

Using the following expressions, find out the values of Θₗ,ₘ(θ) for (i) Θ₁,₀(θ), (ii) Θ₂,₀(θ) and (iii) Θ₂,±₁(θ). [The expressions supplied in the paper are reproduced in the original scan.]

Original printed question · PDF page 2

Ans. 5

Use z=cosθ and the phase convention in the printed paper: Pl|m|(z)=(1−z²)|m|/2d|m|Pl(z)/dz|m|, without a (−1)m factor. The normalized polar factor is

Θl,m(θ)=√[(2l+1)/2 · (l−|m|)!/(l+|m|)!] Pl|m|(cosθ).

For l=1,m=0, Rodrigues’ formula gives P₁(z)=½d(z²−1)/dz=z. Therefore

Θ1,0(θ)=√(3/2) cosθ.

For l=2,m=0, P₂(z)=(1/8)d²(z²−1)²/dz²=(3z²−1)/2. Therefore

Θ2,0(θ)=√(5/8)(3cos²θ−1).

For l=2, |m|=1, P₂¹(z)=√(1−z²)dP₂/dz=3z√(1−z²). The normalization factor is √[(5/2)(1!/3!)]=√(5/12). Thus

Θ2,±1(θ)=(√15/2) sinθ cosθ.

The ± states have azimuthal factors e±iφ/√(2π). A different overall phase, including the Condon–Shortley sign, does not change observables. The printed expression is for Θ; the complete function is Y=Θeimφ/√(2π).

Write down the expressions for the following: Hamiltonian of an one dimensional Harmonic Oscillator.

Original printed question · PDF page 3

Ans. 2(i)

For a particle of mass m with displacement x from equilibrium, the restoring potential is V(x)=½kx²=½mω²x², where ω=√(k/m). The Hamiltonian is kinetic plus potential energy:

Ĥ = −(ℏ²/2m) d²/dx² + ½mω²x².

The allowed energies are Ev=(v+½)ℏω, v=0,1,2,… .

Mid Term · Autumn 2024 · Q2(ii)
PDF page 3 · part of 3 marks · Unit 4
Question

Write down the expressions for the following: Schrödinger eqn. for the hydrogen like atoms.

Original printed question · PDF page 3

Ans. 2(ii)

For one electron and a nucleus of charge +Ze, use the electron–nucleus reduced mass μ. The Coulomb potential is V(r)=−Ze²/(4πε₀r). The time-independent Schrödinger equation is

[−(ℏ²/2μ)∇² − Ze²/(4πε₀r)]ψ(r,θ,φ)=Eψ(r,θ,φ).

For hydrogen Z=1; when the nucleus is treated as fixed, μ≈mₑ. In spherical coordinates,

∇² = (1/r²)∂/∂r(r²∂/∂r)
+ [1/(r²sinθ)]∂/∂θ(sinθ ∂/∂θ)
+ [1/(r²sin²θ)]∂²/∂φ².

The stationary bound-state energies are Eₙ=−μZ²e⁴/[2(4πε₀)²ℏ²n²].

Mid Term · Autumn 2024 · Q3
PDF page 3 · 10 marks · Unit 4
Question

Using the following expressions, find out the values of Θₗ,ₘ(θ) for (i) Θ₁,₀(θ) and (ii) Θ₂,±₁(θ). [See the original scan for the supplied expressions.]

Original printed question · PDF page 3

Ans. 3

Use z=cosθ and the phase convention in the printed paper: Pl|m|(z)=(1−z²)|m|/2d|m|Pl(z)/dz|m|, without a (−1)m factor. The normalized polar factor is

Θl,m(θ)=√[(2l+1)/2 · (l−|m|)!/(l+|m|)!] Pl|m|(cosθ).

For l=1,m=0, Rodrigues’ formula gives P₁(z)=½d(z²−1)/dz=z. Therefore

Θ1,0(θ)=√(3/2) cosθ.

For l=2, |m|=1, P₂¹(z)=√(1−z²)dP₂/dz=3z√(1−z²). The normalization factor is √[(5/2)(1!/3!)]=√(5/12). Thus

Θ2,±1(θ)=(√15/2) sinθ cosθ.

The ± states have azimuthal factors e±iφ/√(2π). A different overall phase, including the Condon–Shortley sign, does not change observables. The printed expression is for Θ; the complete function is Y=Θeimφ/√(2π).

Mid Term · Autumn 2024 · Q4(a)
PDF page 3 · 5 marks · Unit 4
Question

A certain system is described by the Hamiltonian operator H = −d²/dx² + x². (a) Show that ψ = Ax exp(−x²/2) is an eigenfunction of H; determine the eigenvalue.

Original printed question · PDF page 3

Ans. 4(a)

Given Ĥ=−d²/dx²+x² and ψ=Axe−x²/2, differentiate:

ψ′=A(1−x²)e−x²/2,
ψ″=A(x³−3x)e−x²/2.
Ĥψ = −A(x³−3x)e−x²/2 + Ax³e−x²/2 = 3Axe−x²/2 = 3ψ.

ψ is an eigenfunction of Ĥ with eigenvalue 3 (in the dimensionless units of the stated operator).

Mid Term · Autumn 2024 · Q5
PDF page 3 · 5 marks · Unit 4
Question

Using the following expressions, find the radial functions for 2s orbital of hydrogen like atom. [See original scan for supplied expressions.]

Original printed question · PDF page 3

Ans. 5

For the 2s orbital, n=2,l=0. Set ρ=2Zr/(na₀)=Zr/a₀. Write the standard normalized radial solution using the associated Laguerre polynomial:

Rnl(r)=√[(2Z/na₀)³ (n−l−1)!/{2n(n+l)!}]
× e−ρ/2ρlLn−l−12l+1(ρ).

With n=2,l=0, the coefficient is (Z/a₀)3/2/√8 and L₁¹(ρ)=2−ρ. Hence

R20(r)= [1/(2√2)](Z/a₀)3/2(2−Zr/a₀)e−Zr/(2a₀).

For hydrogen, set Z=1. The radial node is at r=2a₀/Z.

This R is normalized by ∫₀∞|R|²r²dr=1. The complete 2s orbital is ψ200=R20Y₀₀=R20/√(4π). The printed paper uses a differently indexed Laguerre convention; the physical radial function is the same up to overall phase.

Test III · November 2023 · Q2
PDF page 4 · 5 marks · Unit 4
Question

Show that for the H-atom, 1s and 2s orbitals are orthogonal. [The two wave functions are given in the scan.]

Original printed question · PDF page 4

Ans. 2

The overlap is S=∫ψ₁ₛ*ψ₂ₛdτ. Both states are spherically symmetric, so integrating the angles yields 4π. Using the supplied normalized functions,

S= [1/(√2 a₀³)]∫₀∞r²(2−r/a₀)e−3r/(2a₀)dr.

Let α=3/(2a₀). The integral is 2·2!/α³−3!/(a₀α⁴)=4/α³−6/(a₀α⁴). Since 4α=6/a₀, this vanishes.

S=[1/(√2 a₀³α⁴)](4α−6/a₀)=0.

The hydrogen 1s and 2s orbitals are orthogonal. ∎

Test III · November 2023 · Q3
PDF page 4 · 4 marks · Unit 4
Question

Prove that [Lₓ, Lᵧ] ≠ 0.

Original printed question · PDF page 4

Ans. 3

For orbital angular momentum, Lₓ=−iℏ(y∂𝓏−z∂ᵧ) and Lᵧ=−iℏ(z∂ₓ−x∂𝓏). Write A=y∂𝓏−z∂ᵧ and B=z∂ₓ−x∂𝓏. Acting on a twice-differentiable test function f, the mixed second-derivative terms cancel, giving

[A,B]f=y∂ₓf−x∂ᵧf.
[Lₓ,Lᵧ]f = (−iℏ)²[A,B]f = ℏ²(x∂ᵧ−y∂ₓ)f = iℏL𝓏f.

[Lₓ,Lᵧ]=iℏL𝓏≠0 as an operator. ∎

Test II · October 2023 · Q1

Question

Using the following expressions, find out the value of Θₗ,ₘ(θ) for Θ₂,±₁(θ). [See the original scan for the expressions.]

Original printed question · PDF page 5

Ans. 1

Use z=cosθ and the phase convention in the printed paper: Pl|m|(z)=(1−z²)|m|/2d|m|Pl(z)/dz|m|, without a (−1)m factor. The normalized polar factor is

Θl,m(θ)=√[(2l+1)/2 · (l−|m|)!/(l+|m|)!] Pl|m|(cosθ).

For l=2, |m|=1, P₂¹(z)=√(1−z²)dP₂/dz=3z√(1−z²). The normalization factor is √[(5/2)(1!/3!)]=√(5/12). Thus

Θ2,±1(θ)=(√15/2) sinθ cosθ.

Test II · October 2023 · Q2
PDF page 5 · 5 marks · Unit 4
Question

For the hydrogen atom, calculate the average distance of the electron from the nucleus in the ground state. [Given: ψ₁ₛ = (1/√π)(1/a₀)³ᐟ² exp(−r/a₀).]

Original printed question · PDF page 5

Ans. 2

For the ground state of hydrogen, ψ₁ₛ=(πa₀³)−1/2e−r/a₀. Use dτ=r²sinθ dr dθ dφ, so angular integration contributes 4π:

⟨r⟩=∫ψ* r ψ dτ=(4/a₀³)∫₀∞r³e−2r/a₀dr.

The integral ∫₀∞rⁿe−αrdr=n!/αn+1. Put n=3 and α=2/a₀:

⟨r⟩=(4/a₀³)·3!/(2/a₀)⁴ = 3a₀/2.

⟨r⟩=1.5a₀≈0.794 Å. This is the mean distance; the most probable radial distance is a₀.

Rnl(r)=√[(2Z/na₀)³ (n−l−1)!/{2n(n+l)!}]
× e−ρ/2ρlLn−l−12l+1(ρ).

With n=2,l=0, the coefficient is (Z/a₀)3/2/√8 and L₁¹(ρ)=2−ρ. Hence

Mid Term · September 2022 · Q1
PDF page 6 · 1 mark · Unit 4
Question

The simple harmonic oscillator was used as a model to explain – (i) excitation of electrons (ii) rotation of molecules (iii) vibration of molecules (iv) polarization of atoms.

Original printed question · PDF page 6

Ans. 1

Correct option: (iii) vibration of molecules. A small displacement q from the equilibrium bond length gives V(q)≈½kq². This is the harmonic-oscillator potential. Molecular rotation is instead described by a rigid rotator.

Mid Term · September 2022 · Q6
PDF page 6 · 1 mark · Unit 4
Question

The components of angular momentum operators commute with each other.

Original printed question · PDF page 6

Ans. 6

False. For different components, [Lₓ,Lᵧ]=iℏL𝓏 and cyclic analogues. Thus two different components generally cannot have simultaneous sharp values.

Mid Term · September 2022 · Q7
PDF page 6 · 1 mark · Unit 4
Question

The spin angular momentum operators are linear and Hermitian.

Original printed question · PDF page 6

Ans. 7

True. Spin components represent observables, so they are linear Hermitian operators. For spin ½, Sᵢ=(ℏ/2)σᵢ; each Pauli matrix equals its conjugate transpose.

They nevertheless do not mutually commute: [Sₓ,Sᵧ]=iℏS𝓏.

Mid Term · September 2022 · Q8
PDF page 6 · 1 mark · Unit 4
Question

The energy of a rigid rotator is independent of its mass.

Original printed question · PDF page 6

Ans. 8

False. EJ=ℏ²J(J+1)/(2I), where I=μr². The reduced mass μ=m₁m₂/(m₁+m₂) explicitly affects the energy. At fixed geometry, increasing μ decreases the rotational spacings.

Test III · November 2022 · Q4
PDF page 7 · 4 marks · Unit 4
Question

The microwave spectrum of H³⁵Cl consists of a series of equally spaced lines separated by 6.26×10¹¹ Hz. Calculate the bond length of H³⁵Cl.

Original printed question · PDF page 7

Ans. 4

For a rigid rotator, EJ=h²J(J+1)/(8π²I). Allowed transitions have ΔJ=+1, so

νJ→J+1=h(J+1)/(4π²I).

Successive line frequencies are separated by Δν=h/(4π²I). The stated spacing, 6.26×10¹¹ Hz, therefore gives

I=h/(4π²Δν)=2.68116×10−47 kg m².

For H³⁵Cl, use μ=(1×35)/(1+35)u=1.61441×10−27 kg. Since I=μr²,

r=√(I/μ)=√[(2.68116×10−47)/(1.61441×10−27)]
=1.28871×10−10 m.

Bond length ≈1.29 Å using mass-number approximations.

Selection audit

Included

PDF pages 1, 2, 3, 5 and 6: all quantum-paper questions. Page 4: Q2 and Q3 only. Page 7: Q4 only. Spin-component operators are included under angular momentum; hydrogen radial and angular functions are included under the hydrogen atom.

Excluded as outside the uploaded syllabus
  • Page 4, Q1(i) and Q1(ii): perturbation theory and Hartree–Fock theory.
  • Page 7, Q1–Q3: Born–Oppenheimer approximation, variation theorem, spin orbitals and the Li-atom Slater determinant.
  • Pages 8–10: inorganic-chemistry questions, including VSEPR, halogens, ligand-field spectra, transition-metal electronic terms and microstates. These require material beyond the listed single-particle/angular-momentum topics.
  • Pages 11–15 and 18: thermodynamics, solutions, chemical equilibrium and physical chemistry.
  • Pages 16, 17 and 19: organic reactions, pericyclic chemistry, amino acids and stereochemistry.
Some syllabus topics have no matching PYQ in this PDF: Franck–Hertz, Compton scattering, wave–particle duality, uncertainty, and dedicated free-particle derivations. No invented question has been presented as a PYQ.
